opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Samuel. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'll give you the version I'd say on stage and the version I'd say to my board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a productivity tool and we're using it to serve clients better. The standard line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a little disappointing. If everyone gets the same small boost, nobody gains an edge. I want an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep rolling out tools in bidding and scheduling. Keep costs tight. Watch what the big players do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, if anything.

S0.say: AI is a productivity tool, and we're using it to serve clients better.
S0.think: A little disappointing. If everyone gets the same boost, nobody gets an edge.
S0.do: Rolls out tools in bidding and scheduling, keeps costs tight and watches the big players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're taking a measured approach. Clients like hearing 'measured'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow suits a mid-size firm fine. The danger is a big rival moving faster than everyone else and pricing me out. Ten years is plenty of time to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hire fewer juniors and let the tools do the routine work. Put real money into automating our bids, because winning tenders is where speed pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. Not worried yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire fewer juniors yourself. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's a business. I'd keep the best ones.

S1.think: Slow suits us, unless a big rival moves faster and prices me out.
S1.do: Hires fewer juniors and puts real money into automating bids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're investing in our people and in new roles. Which we would be, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is good for us if we move first. My back office could run on a third of the staff. I'd cut it, win more bids on price and put the savings back in. The politicians can argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut the admin, finance and planning teams down over the year. Use the savings to undercut rivals on two or three big tenders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. This is the opening I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In public you'd say you're investing in your people. In private you'd cut two thirds of the back office. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd invest in the ones who stay. The rest get a fair package. That's how business works.

S2.say: We're investing in our people and in new roles.
S2.think: This is good if we move first. My back office could run on a third of the staff.
S2.do: Cuts admin, finance and planning staff over the year and uses the savings to undercut rivals on big tenders.
S2.feel: Good. The opening he's been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort out who gets the gains, and government should be careful not to kill growth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shares and property go up a lot, so personally I'm fine. What worries me is the big service companies automating their engineering faster than me, and the political fight ending in heavy taxes on people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push automation hard across engineering and bidding. Sit down with my advisers about protecting the family's assets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about money. About losing the race.

S3.say: The market will sort out who gets the gains. Government shouldn't kill growth.
S3.think: Personally I'm fine. The worry is bigger rivals automating faster, and heavy taxes on people like me.
S3.do: Pushes automation hard across engineering and bidding, and talks to advisers about protecting the family's assets.
S3.feel: Uneasy about losing the race, not about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots will make field work safer and more efficient. Every CEO would say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the race I was afraid of. Robots on rigs and in the yard cost a lot up front. The giants can buy whole fleets. I'd have to borrow or partner to keep up, or sell to one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the robot makers in the first month. Trial a few units on our biggest contract. Quietly sound out a buyer in case we can't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Part excited, part worried I'll be too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would selling the company feel like a loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money-wise, no. I'd be fine. Pride-wise, yes. I built it to win, not to sell.

S4.say: Robots will make field work safer and more efficient.
S4.think: The giants can buy whole fleets. I'd have to borrow or partner to keep up, or sell.
S4.do: Meets robot makers in the first month, trials units on the biggest contract and quietly sounds out a buyer.
S4.feel: Wired. Part excited, part worried about being too slow.
